questions.q: In emit<K extends EventName<E>>(name: K, ...args: PayloadArgs<E[K]>), what decides which payload type the call accepts?
questions.explain: K is inferred from the string literal you pass, and E[K] looks up that one event's payload in the map. The name decides. If the caller or a listener could pick the type, it would be a claim that nothing checks.
options: The type argument the caller writes, as in emit<OrderPlaced>(…)
The event name passed as the first argument, from which K is inferred
The type of the first listener that was registered for that name
Nothing: E[K] is always the union of every payload

questions.q: With new EventEmitter<ShopEvents>() from node:events, shop.on("order.created", (order) => …) compiled although the map only has "order.placed". Why?
questions.explain: Node's typings are deliberately open: an unknown name is allowed, and its listener parameters are any. The map helps with known names but cannot make a typo an error. A bus whose on only accepts keyof E can.
options: The event map was declared as an interface instead of a type alias
TypeScript cannot check string arguments at all
Node's types accept any event name so emitters can carry unlisted events, and for an unknown name the listener's arguments are any
Because "order.created" and "order.placed" share the namespace order

questions.q: The map has "cart.cleared": void, and emit takes ...args: PayloadArgs<E[K]> with type PayloadArgs<P> = [P] extends [void] ? [] : [payload: P]. Which call compiles?
questions.explain: For void the rest parameter is the empty tuple [], so the call takes no payload at all. Any second argument, even undefined, is "expected 1 arguments, but got 2".
options: shop.emit("cart.cleared")
shop.emit("cart.cleared", undefined)
shop.emit("cart.cleared", {})
All three

questions.q: Why is PayloadArgs written [P] extends [void] instead of P extends void?
questions.explain: A conditional type on a naked type parameter runs once per union member. For a payload like { note: string } | void the naked version would give [] | [payload: { note: string }], silently making the payload optional. Wrapping both sides in a tuple switches distribution off.
options: The bracket form is faster to compile
A naked P would distribute over a union payload and produce a union of argument lists; the brackets ask one question about the whole type
P extends void is a syntax error
The brackets make the payload optional for every event

questions.q: Why does this compile, although it sends a cancellation payload to the "stock.low" listeners?
questions.explain: This is the correlated-union problem. The pairing between a name and its payload exists only in your head once they are two union-typed variables. Keep them in one EventOf value instead.
options: Because emit has a bug in its implementation
K is inferred as the whole union, so E[K] is the union of both payloads, and two separate variables no longer know they belong together
Because object literals are never checked for extra properties in function calls
Because ShopEvents is an interface

questions.q: What is the best way to make forward refuse a mismatched name and payload?
questions.explain: Each member of EventOf ties one name to its payload, so a mismatched pair matches no member and is refused. A generic K helps literal callers, but a caller holding a union name would reopen the hole; the cast only hides it.
options: Add as const to the call
Cast the payload: emit(name, payload as ShopEvents[typeof name])
Take one parameter of type EventOf<ShopEvents, "order.cancelled" | "stock.low">, a union of { name, payload } objects
Make forward generic with <K extends keyof ShopEvents> and keep both parameters

questions.q: The bus stores all listeners in one Map<string, Set<Stored>> and casts each listener on the way in. Why can this cast not be avoided?
questions.explain: Map<keyof E, Listener<E[keyof E]>> would say "any listener under any name". The honest design is a typed public API over loosely typed storage, with the single cast at the point where precise types enter it, justified because emit checks the arguments per name.
options: Because Map cannot hold functions
TypeScript has no type for a map whose value type depends on the key, so the per-name listener types cannot be expressed in one collection
Because private fields cannot have generic types
It can: Map<keyof E, Listener<E[keyof E]>> is exact

questions.q: Why does emit loop over [...set] instead of the live collection?
questions.explain: once listeners remove themselves while emit is running. With an array that would skip the next listener; with a live Set, a listener added during the loop would also run. Iterating over a snapshot avoids both.
options: Copying makes the loop faster
Sets cannot be iterated with for…of
A listener may unsubscribe itself or subscribe another during the loop; a copy makes each emit call exactly the listeners that existed when it started
To prevent the listeners from changing the payload

questions.q: With the lesson's onPattern, what does a listener for "order.*" receive?
questions.explain: A wildcard listener receives several kinds of event, so it gets EventOf<E, Matching<E, "order.*">>. Checking event.name narrows event.payload to that event's type.
options: The payload of the first order event in the map
A value of type unknown
A union of { name, payload } objects, one for each event whose name starts with order., which it narrows by checking name
An intersection of all order payloads

questions.q: A plugin subscribes with bus.onPattern(`${moduleName}.*`, …) where moduleName: string. What happens?
questions.explain: Types only know values known at compile time. A pattern built from a plain string could be anything, so the typed method refuses it. You must check the value at runtime and cast, or use an untyped method. This is one of the real limits of typed wildcards.
options: It compiles and matches every event
It does not compile: the pattern's type is `${string}.*`, which is not one of the known Pattern<E> literals
It compiles, and the listener receives never
TypeScript evaluates moduleName at compile time

questions.q: Why does the lesson's bus refuse onPattern("*.placed", …)?
questions.explain: The type-level pattern language and the runtime matcher must agree. Every extra form ("any namespace", "one level only") has to be added to both, which is why a small pattern language is the practical choice.
options: Because * is not allowed inside string literal types
Because no event ends in .placed
Because the Pattern type only describes "*" and "namespace.*"; a new pattern form needs new type machinery and matching runtime code
Because wildcards must always come last in JavaScript strings

questions.q: Why does the bus use Promise.allSettled rather than Promise.all to run async listeners?
questions.explain: For error isolation the publisher needs every outcome: which listeners succeeded, which failed and why. allSettled reports each result as fulfilled or rejected.
options: Promise.all runs listeners one after another
Promise.all rejects as soon as one listener fails, so the publisher learns about one failure and loses the results of the others; allSettled waits for all and never rejects
Promise.allSettled cancels failing listeners
Only allSettled accepts async functions

questions.q: The bus runs calls.map(async (call) => call()). What would go wrong with calls.map((call) => call())?
questions.explain: An async function never throws; it returns a rejected promise. The wrapper converts a synchronous throw into a rejection, so it is isolated and reported like any async failure.
options: Nothing; the async is only for readability
Async listeners would never finish
A listener that throws synchronously would throw out of map, so the listeners after it would never be called and allSettled would never see the failure
The results would come back in the wrong order

questions.q: A worker reads events from a message queue and publishes them on the typed bus. What does the event map guarantee about those payloads?
questions.explain: Types are erased and never inspect data. The map describes what the program expects; a validator per event name checks what actually arrived.
options: That they match the map, because publish only accepts EventOf<E>
Nothing at runtime: JSON.parse returns any, so each payload must be checked by a runtime validator before it is published
That unknown event names are dropped automatically
That numbers arrive as numbers

questions.q: What does annotating the validators object as { readonly [K in EventName<E>]: (payload: unknown) => payload is E[K] } buy you?
questions.explain: The mapped type turns "every event needs a validator" into a compile-time rule. The validators still do the actual checking at runtime.
options: It generates the validators automatically
Adding an event to the map makes the validators object fail to compile until it has a validator for the new name, with the right guard type
It checks the payloads at compile time instead of runtime
It makes the validators run faster

questions.q: Why does parseEvent check the incoming name with Object.hasOwn(validators, name) rather than name in validators?
questions.explain: An object literal inherits from Object.prototype. "toString" in validators is true. Names from outside the program must be checked against the object's own keys only.
options: in does not work with string keys
They are identical; it is a style choice
in also finds inherited keys such as "toString", so a message named "toString" would look like a known event
Object.hasOwn also validates the payload

questions.q: With @zudojs/events, bus.on<Event<OrderPlaced>>("stock.low", handler) compiles. What is the type argument?
questions.explain: A type argument that only describes what a callback will receive works like as. The package's event types are plain strings, so it cannot link names to payloads; a small typed layer that takes your map as a type parameter can.
options: A check: the bus verifies that "stock.low" carries an OrderPlaced
A claim: nothing connects it to the event name, so the handler is told it receives an OrderPlaced whatever arrives
A runtime filter that skips events of other shapes
A default that is replaced by the real payload type when the event is registered

questions.q: EventUnion<ShopEvents> from @zudojs/events fails with "Index signature for type 'string' is missing" when ShopEvents is an interface. Why?
questions.explain: An interface can be extended later by declaration merging, so TypeScript will not assume it has only string keys with unknown values. A type alias is closed, so it is assignable to Record<string, unknown>.
options: Interfaces cannot have string literal keys
Its constraint is Record<string, unknown>, and interfaces do not get an implicit index signature, while type aliases of object literal types do
The package needs the map to be declared with as const
Because the payload void is not allowed

questions.q: What is the advantage of accepting { signal?: AbortSignal } in on?
questions.explain: AbortSignal is the platform's shared cancellation token. Tying listeners to it means cleanup happens in one place instead of keeping every unsubscribe function around.
options: It makes the listener run faster
It lets the listener cancel the event for other listeners
One signal, such as the one for an HTTP request, can remove every listener, timer and fetch that request started when it ends, which prevents listener leaks
It is required for async listeners

questions.q: Checkout needs to know whether charging the card succeeded before it shows the receipt. Is an event the right tool?
questions.explain: An event says "this happened" and does not care who listens. When you need an answer, or a guarantee that exactly one piece of code ran, you want a command or query, the topic of the next lesson.
options: Yes: emit "card.charge" and read the listener's return value
No: events announce something that already happened, may have zero or many listeners and return no answer; a command with exactly one handler and a typed result fits
Yes, as long as the listener is async
No, because events cannot carry amounts

questions.q: You must rename totalKobo to amountKobo in the order.placed payload, and another service reads these events from a queue. What is the safe approach?
questions.explain: The compiler only sees code compiled with yours. Listeners in other services, and messages already sitting in the queue, still have the old shape. A new event name lets old and new consumers coexist during the change.
options: Rename the field; TypeScript will find every listener
Rename the field and bump the package version
Publish a new event such as order.placed.v2 with the new shape alongside the old one until every listener has moved
Make both fields optional

questions.q: A type test file contains // @ts-expect-error above shop.emit("order.created", payload). When does tsc fail on that file?
questions.explain: The directive expects an error on the next line. If there is none, tsc reports an unused directive. So the file proves that the API keeps refusing what it should.
options: Always, because the line has an error
When the line stops being an error, for example after someone loosens emit to accept any string
Only when the event name is misspelled differently
Never; the directive silences everything

questions.q: Why can it be useful to declare the event map as an interface rather than a type alias?
questions.explain: Interfaces merge: declare module "./shop-events.js" { interface ShopEvents { "loyalty.earned": … } } adds a name. That only works for code known at compile time, and it is also why an interface does not satisfy a Record<string, unknown> constraint.
options: Interfaces allow number keys
A plugin package can add events to it with module augmentation (declaration merging)
Interfaces are checked at runtime
Type aliases cannot have string literal keys

questions.explain: The prefix is "order." including the dot, so "orders.synced" and the bare "order" do not match, and the deeper "order.item.added" does. The type-level `order.${string}` matches the same names, because ${string} can contain dots.
options: order | order.placed | orders.synced | order.item.added
order.placed

questions.explain: It compiles because inside forward, K is the whole union and the payload may be either shape. At runtime the stock handler reads e.sku from a cancellation payload and gets undefined. Reading a missing property is not an error in JavaScript, so the bug is silent.

questions.explain: in walks the prototype chain and finds Object.prototype.toString. Object.hasOwn only looks at the object's own keys, which is what you want for names that come from outside.

questions.explain: In @zudojs/events a namespace pattern also matches the bare namespace ("order") and every depth below it, but not "orders.synced", because it matches whole segments. questions.explain: A promise settles once; later calls to resolve are ignored, so the value is ORD-1. But the listener is still registered: every waitFor call leaves one dead listener behind. That is why the lesson builds waitFor on once, which unsubscribes.

questions.explain: The public signature does the checking: K comes from the name, and PayloadArgs<E[K]> is empty for "cart.cleared". Inside, the listeners are stored loosely, so spreading args into them needs no further cast.

questions.q: Write matches(pattern, name): "*" matches every name, "ns.*" matches names that start with ns. (at any depth, but not ns itself or nss.x), and any other pattern must equal the name. The program should print order.placed,order.item.added, stock.low and 5.
questions.explain: Keeping the dot in the prefix ("order.") is what stops "orders.synced" from matching. Whatever rule you choose, the type-level Matching must describe the same set of names.

questions.q: Finish emitAll. It calls every listener with the SKU, waits for all of them, isolates failures (synchronous throws and rejected promises alike) and returns how many were delivered and how many failed. The program should print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: The async wrapper converts the synchronous throw into a rejection, and allSettled waits for every listener. Without the wrapper, the second listener's throw would escape map and the last listener would never run.

questions.q: Events arrive as JSON from a queue. Write the type guard isStockLow: the payload must be an object with a string sku and a whole-number left that is 0 or more. The program should print ok RICE-50KG 3 and then rejected three times.
questions.explain: The event map says left is a number, but only a runtime check can refuse "3", -1 or null. Number.isInteger is false for strings, so it checks the type and the value at once.

questions.q: Add waitFor(name) to the emitter. It returns a promise of that event's payload, resolves on the next event with that name, and unsubscribes itself so only one event is consumed. The program should print 1, 0 and PSK_1042 1500000.
questions.explain: The listener removes itself before resolving, so the second emit finds no listener (0). K is inferred from the name, so the promise is typed with that event's payload and payment.reference is checked. The Promise.race in the program only stops an unfinished answer from waiting forever.

questions.q: Write the mapped type Formatters<E>: one formatter per event name, taking that event's payload and returning a string. Then finish describe. The program should print order.placed: ORD-9 ₦7000 and stock.low: OIL-5L x1.
questions.explain: With the mapped type, a missing formatter or a formatter that reads the wrong payload is a compile error, and the parameters no longer need annotations: each is typed from its key. Inside the generic describe, TypeScript cannot prove that formatters[name] takes ShopEvents[K], so one cast connects them.

questions.q: Put a typed layer over @zudojs/events: on(type, handler) and publish(type, payload) take the name from ShopEvents and derive the payload from it. publish returns how many handlers ran. The program should print the four lines shown.
questions.explain: The package's on<Event<P>> is a claim, but inside on the claim is derived from the same K as the name, so callers can no longer make a wrong one. publishEvent builds the event and returns a report with handlerCount.

1
thank you for ORD-1

questions.q: Finish on so that it stores the listener and records one warning the moment a name gets more than max listeners, like Node's leak warning. The program should print possible leak: 4 listeners for order.placed.
questions.explain: Subscribing once per request (the loop) is the classic leak. Warning exactly when the count first passes the limit, and not again for every further listener, keeps the log readable. No type can catch a leak; it is a runtime property.
